title: Dunes
escapeBrief: To get out you worked out the day and hour you could walk across to the stranded water steamer. It is 1928; the river has not flooded in two years, the company has abandoned the town and stopped the water shipments, and its last steamer, carrying a sea-water condenser for the town, lies on the far side of a breach the storm cut through the sand spit. The bar at the mouth of the breach can be waded only when the water over it falls below the wading line, which needs every rhythm of the sea to line up in daylight, perhaps once in weeks, for about an hour; nobody can wait down there, because the town has no water to spare and the strandwolves work the beach at night. The town engineer built a tide machine to predict that hour, and a storm scattered its four pulleys. You found them in the general store, on the cliff winch, in the dunes and on the flats, and fitted them to the machine's four shafts: the moon, the sun, the moon's near-and-far, and the afternoon wind. A bigger pulley swings the wire further, so which pulley goes on which shaft says how much each rhythm moves the water. The lore told you the moon pulls hardest and that its near-and-far pulls less than the sun, which left three ways to fit them. Cranking the machine back to the dates in the engineer's logbook showed which one puts the pen where he measured the water. Cranking forward, the pen first dips below the wading line at night, which is no use; the first daylight dip is 28 June at first light, when the wind is calmest, and that is the day and hour you set on his alarm clock. The printed company tide table, which everyone in town trusts, was worked out with no wind at all, so its spring low sends you down at midday with the southerly piling water over the bar. Adding up several inputs, each weighted by how much it matters, and checking the result against what was measured, is exactly what a multiple regression does, on the machine or in R.
